title: The Dentist
strapline: Open wide! Let's count those teeth, give them a good brush, and take the fear out of the dentist's chair.
intent: A trip to the dentist can feel daunting, so playing it out helps children feel calm, prepared and in control of an experience many find worrying.
The dentist is a real community helper, and the role play builds knowledge of the people who keep us healthy and of how to look after our own bodies.
Counting teeth, brushing in order and looking after the 'patients' weaves in mathematics and important self-care habits.
Caring for worried patients — reassuring them, explaining gently — grows empathy, communication and emotional understanding.
Children learn genuine, useful health knowledge — why we brush, what's good and not good for teeth, why we visit the dentist — through play, not lecture.
Real vocabulary flows in — dentist, teeth, brush, healthy, examine, appointment, gentle, check-up.
implementation: Set up a dentist's surgery — a chair, mirrors, a big model of teeth or a picture, toothbrushes, masks, an appointment book and a waiting area.
Take the patient role, sometimes a nervous one, so children reassure, explain and care: 'It won't hurt — I'm just going to count your teeth. Ready?'
Model the health talk: 'Let's check these teeth are being brushed well. How many can you count on the top?'
Bring in maths through the play — count and number the teeth, brush in a careful order, use a timer for the two-minute brush.
Weave in real knowledge kindly — what helps teeth stay strong, sometimes-foods and everyday-foods, why check-ups matter — and read tooth-themed stories.
Add an appointment book and reminder cards for real writing, and invite a dental visitor or send toothbrushing charts home to families.
key_questions: How many teeth can you count on the top?
It won't hurt — I'm just going to count your teeth. Are you ready?
Which foods help our teeth stay strong, and which are just sometimes-foods?
How long should we brush for — shall we set the timer?
What do you say to the patient who feels a bit worried?

impact.text: Children take control of a worrying experience in the safety of role play, feeling calm and prepared.
Children learn about a community helper and how to look after their own bodies.
Children count and number the teeth and brush in a careful order.
Children care for worried patients — reassuring and explaining gently — growing empathy and communication.
Children take on real health knowledge — why we brush, good and sometimes-foods, why we visit.
